title: Adjectives
goal: Use adjectives in both their forms, master the one exception that decides everything, and compare two things.
bekal: knowing when an adjective gets **-e** and when it doesn't
describing what someone looks like and what they're like
wave: Go back to **unit 13**: write ten requests for help, from the most casual to the most polite, all with modal verbs.

dialogs.title: Dialog — Op het station
dialogs.intro: Budi is picking up a cousin he has never met, with only one clue: "you'll recognize him for sure."

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.id: What does your cousin look like?

lines.speaker: Tante:
lines.text: Hij is lang en heeft donker haar.
lines.id: He's tall and has dark hair.
lines.literal: he is long and has dark hair.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Dat is de helft van Nederland niet.
lines.id: That's half the Netherlands, isn't it.
lines.literal: that is the half of the-Netherlands not.

lines.speaker: Tante:
lines.text: Hij draagt een rode jas en een grijze rugzak.
lines.id: He's wearing a red coat and a gray backpack.
lines.literal: he wears a red coat and a gray backpack.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.id: A red coat — now that helps.

lines.speaker: Tante:
lines.text: En hij heeft een klein kind bij zich.
lines.id: And he has a small child with him.
lines.literal: and he has a small child by himself.

lines.speaker: Tante:
lines.text: Goed opgelet. Het is een het-woord.
lines.literal: well noticed. it is a het-word.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Maar het kleine kind wél met -e?
lines.id: But het kleine kind does take -e?
lines.literal: but the small child indeed with -e?

lines.speaker: Tante:
lines.text: Precies. Alleen bij een is er geen -e.
lines.id: Exactly. Only after een is there no -e.
lines.literal: precisely. only at een is there no -e.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Dat is de gekste regel tot nu toe.
lines.id: That's the craziest rule so far.
lines.literal: that is the craziest rule till-now.

notes: **Hoe ziet hij eruit?** — *eruitzien* (to look, appear). The answer can go two ways: looks (*hij is lang*) or clothes (*hij draagt een rode jas*).

**Donker haar** without *-e*? That's right — *haar* is a het-word (*het haar*), and here it stands with no article at all. A singular het-word without *de/het* behaves just like one after *een*: the adjective stays bare.
**Een rode jas** — *de jas* is a de-word, so the adjective takes *-e*. Note the spelling too: *rood* → *rode* (one *o* drops), following the open-syllable rule from unit 3.
**Een klein kind** — *het kind* is a het-word preceded by *een*, so the adjective has **no** *-e*. This is the only exception in the whole Dutch adjective rule.
**Het kleine kind** — as soon as the article is *het* (not *een*), the *-e* comes back. Same with *dit kleine kind*, *mijn kleine kind*.
**Goed opgelet** — short praise, from *opletten* (to pay attention). *Let op!* means "watch out!" and is written on every Dutch warning sign.
**De gekste regel** — the superlative: *gek → gekker → gekst*. Note the *de* in front; the superlative almost always takes an article.

grammars.title: When an adjective gets -e
body: The rule is short: **an adjective before a noun almost always gets -e.** There is one exception, and one situation where it doesn't change at all.
after: Row four is the whole difficulty: *een groot huis*, *een klein kind*, *een lekker broodje*. If the word before it isn't *een* — but *het*, *dit*, *dat*, *mijn*, *ons* — the *-e* comes back: *ons grote huis*.
The last row matters too: after *zijn*, *worden*, *blijven*, the adjective stands alone with no ending. *De koffie is lekker.*
Adjectives ending in *-en* never change: *een gouden ring*, *houten tafel*. Nor do *plastic*, *oranje*, *roze*.

grammars.title: Comparing
body: Just as tidy as English, with the same three irregular words.
after: "More … than" = **-er … dan**: *Amsterdam is groter **dan** Utrecht.* "As … as" = *even … als* or *net zo … als*: *Utrecht is **even** mooi **als** Amsterdam.*
The superlative takes an article: *de mooiste stad*, *het grootste huis*, or *het … -st* after a verb: *In juli is het weer **het mooist**.*
*Liever* and *het liefst* express preference: *Ik drink **liever** thee* (I'd rather drink tea). This will come in very handy in the next unit.

blocks.text: ⚠️ *Knap* means good-looking **and** clever, depending on context. *Wat knap van je!* means "well done!", not a comment on your looks.

blocks.title: Colors
items: *Rood → rode*, *wit → witte*, *zwart → zwarte* — the spelling follows the long/short vowel rule.
⚠️ **Oranje** is more than a color in the Netherlands: it's the color of the royal family (Oranje-Nassau) and the national team. On *Koningsdag*, April 27, the whole country dresses in orange.

blocks.text: *Lekker* goes far beyond "tasty" for food: *lekker weer* (lovely weather), *lekker slapen* (sleep soundly), *lekker bezig* (happily busy with something). It's one of the words the Dutch say most in a day.

*Gezellig* is the most famous untranslatable Dutch word. It means warm, close, cozy, and enjoyable all at once — and it works for a room, an afternoon, a café, or a person. *Wat gezellig!* is said when someone comes to visit; *het was heel gezellig* when they leave. If you learn one word from this unit, make it this one.

items: Dit is de ____ stad van Nederland. (mooi)
Thee is ____ dan koffie voor mij. (goed)

exercises.prompt: Put the words in the right order.

answers: groot — grote — lange — rode — klein — warm — mooie — groot
Hij is lang en heeft donker haar. — Hij draagt een rode jas. — Het kleine huis is mooi. — Dit is een groot huis. — Utrecht is rustiger dan Amsterdam. — Het was heel gezellig.
Hij draagt een rode jas. — Dat is een groot huis. — Amsterdam is groter dan Utrecht. — Het was erg gezellig. — Hoe ziet hij eruit?
